title: Nanoporous structured Sn-MWCNT/Cu electrodes fabricated by electrodeposition–chemical dezincification for catalytic CO2 reduction
abstract: Funding information Guangxi Technology Base and Talent Subject, Grant/Award Number: GUIKE AD18126001; International Academic Cooperation and Exchange Program of Shanghai Science and Technology Committee, Grant/Award Number: 18160723600; Special Fund for Guangxi Distinguished Expert Summary A facile method is developed to fabricate nanoporous, structured, Sn-based catalyst electrodes. Sn, Zn, and multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are coelectrodeposited on a copper substrate, followed by chemical dezincification in NaOH aqueous solution to remove Zn. By controlling variables such as the contents of Zn and MWCNTs, a series of Sn-MWCNT/Cu (SZMC) electrodes are fabricated. Experimental results show that using such novel SZMC electrodes can achieve a HCOO Faradaic efficiency of over 91% at −0.99 V versus RHE for 10 hours in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. The high performance is attributed to the addition of MWCNTs and Zn, followed by chemical dezincification to remove Zn and then create vacancies in the catalyst structure, which results in a special porous structure of SZMC with large surface area. Then ECSA is used for enhancing the catalytic activity and selectivity of HCOO production, as well as promoting intermediate adsorption and mass transfer.

R E S E A R CH AR T I C L E
Nanoporous structured Sn-MWCNT/Cu electrodes fabricated by electrodeposition–chemical dezincification for catalytic CO2 reduction
Xiaolin Shao | Qi Zhang | Xurui Zhang | Jin Yi | Yuyu Liu |
Jiujun Zhang
Institute for Sustainable Energy/College of Sciences, Shanghai University, Shanghai, China

Summary
A facile method is developed to fabricate nanoporous, structured, Sn-based cat-
alyst electrodes. Sn, Zn, and multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are co-
electrodeposited on a copper substrate, followed by chemical dezincification in
NaOH aqueous solution to remove Zn. By controlling variables such as the
contents of Zn and MWCNTs, a series of Sn-MWCNT/Cu (SZMC) electrodes
are fabricated. Experimental results show that using such novel SZMC electrodes can achieve a HCOO− Faradaic efficiency of over 91% at −0.99 V versus RHE for 10 hours in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. The high
performance is attributed to the addition of MWCNTs and Zn, followed by
chemical dezincification to remove Zn and then create vacancies in the cata-
lyst structure, which results in a special porous structure of SZMC with large
surface area. Then ECSA is used for enhancing the catalytic activity and selectivity of HCOO− production, as well as promoting intermediate adsorption and
mass transfer.

sections.heading: 1 | INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The rapid economic development and population growth are speeding up the consumption of fossil fuels for energy and emitting more CO2 and other pollutants into atmosphere, which have been causing the fast exhaustion of unsustainable energy sources and environmental pollution at the same time.1,2 To mitigate these energy and environmental issues, efforts in exploring clean and sustainable energy sources such as solar, wind, waterfall, sea-wave, geothermal, etc., as well as the corresponding energy storage and conversion technologies, have become extensive in the last several decades.3,4 Among the different technologies explored, CO2 conversion to produce
low-carbon fuels and value-added chemicals has received great attention recently.5,6 Particularly, electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ERCO2) can not only store electrical energy from renewable sources but also produce useful fuels for many applications.7-9 As recognized, ERCO2 has some favorable features, such as the mild operation condition, controllable product, and adjustable reaction system.10-12 However, high-performance and selective electrocatalysts are needed to speed up ERCO2 to practical rates.
Normally, different types of electrocatalysts can catalyze ERCO2 to produce different low-carbon products, including HCOO−,13 CO,14,15 CH4, 16,17 CH3OH, 18 C2H4, 19 etc. Among these products, HCOO− is a very valuable

DOI: 10.1002/er.6250
Int J Energy Res. 2020;1–12. wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/er © 2020 John Wiley & Sons Ltd 1
chemical and widely used in printing, dyeing, medicine, textiles, and fuel cells.20,21 As reported, the Cu-, Bi-, Sb-, and Sn-based electrocatalysts could selectively catalyze ERCO2 to HCOO
−.22-24 In this regard, Sn as a nontoxic and nonprecious metal has attracted much attention with high selectivity, cost effectiveness, environmental friendliness, and stability.20,25 So far, some impressive results have been achieved with Sn-based catalysts for ERCO2, as summarized in Table S1. The morphology of the material has a very important effect on the performance of the catalyst.26,27 For example, a wavy SnO2 with optimized surface structure was developed that showed good activity toward HCOO− product.28 Liu et al29 developed SnO2 quantum wires with a size below 2 nm as electrocatalyst to catalyze the conversion of ERCO2 into HCOO
− with a Faradaic efficiency (FEHCOO− ) of over 80%, and attributed the higher performance (compared to that of SnO2 nanoparticles) to the larger electrochemically active surface area. Creating a porous structure is one of the methods to improve the performance of a catalyst, because porous materials have larger specific surface area and electrochemically active surface area than planar materials; also, the porous structure is conducive to the transfer of CO2 molecules.
23,30 Han et al31 prepared SnO2 nanosheets with a special hierarchical mesoporous structure for catalyzing ERCO2 to HCOO
− with a high FEHCOO− of 83%. Besides, Kuang et al.
32 obtained hierarchically porous SnO2-coupled organic carbon and attributed the preferential adsorption and activation of CO2 (FEHCOO− reached 75% and FEcarbon products reached 95%) to the special structure. However, the process of pore formation is very complicated and even needs to be carried out at high temperatures. Hence, an efficient catalyst with simple synthesis method needs to be developed.
In our continuous effort to simplify the synthesis method and achieve high-efficiency catalysts for ERCO2, a two-step synthesis under mild conditions, that is, Sn/Zn/MWCNT co-electrodeposition on Cu substrate followed by an alkali dezincification, is explored, and a series of nanoporous structured Sn-MWCNT/Cu (SZMC, hereafter) electrodes were successfully obtained, as listed in Table S2. By characterization through X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and other analytical techniques, as well as by electrochemical performance tests, the morphological structure and electrochemical performance of such a series of electrodes are compared. Among them, SZ0.5MC with both MWCNTs and a porous structure showed the best performance with a HCOO− Faradaic efficiency of over 91% at −0.99 V versus RHE and long-term stability for 10 hours in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution with 20 mA/cm
2, and is superior to those reported in most literature (Table S1).

sections.heading: 2.1 | Materials
sections.text: Cu foil, multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), and sodium hydroxide were purchased from Shanghai Titan Scientific Co., Ltd., China; stannic chloride was supplied by Adamas Reagent Co., Ltd., China; zinc sulfate heptahydrate was acquired from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co., Ltd., China; and hydrochloric acid was from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., China. All reagents were analytical grade and used without further purification. All experimental solutions were prepared in deionized water.

sections.heading: 2.2 | Fabrication of electrodes
sections.text:
A 0.1-mm-thick, 2 cm × 2 cm Cu foil was polished with 100 grade abrasive paper, washed in water and ethanol, and then sonicated in dilute hydrochloric acid for 10 minutes. In the SZ0.5MC electrode fabrication process, the electrodeposition solution was prepared by 10 mM SnCl2, 0.5 mM ZnSO4 7H2O, and 250 mg/L MWCNTs. By using a constant current density of 30 mA/cm2 for 1 hour, which was applied by a regulated dc power supply (linear dc power; Longwei Instruments, HK Co., Ltd., China), the electrodeposition of Sn, Zn, and MWCNTs was carried out on the pretreated copper foil. Subsequently, the obtained material was washed with deionized water and then leached in 50 mM NaOH aqueous solution for 8 hours dezincification (the whole preparation is shown in Scheme 1). Also, a series of SZMC, S0MC, SZC, and S0C electrodes were fabricated via co-electrodeposition of different amounts of ZnSO4 and MWCNTs at current densities (jel) varying from 20 to 40 mA/cm
2, followed by 0–14 hours (tal) alkali leaching for dezincification (Table S2).

sections.heading: 2.3 | Characterization of electrodes
sections.text: The crystalline structures of the electrodes were studied by an X-ray diffractometer (Ultima IV, Japan) with Cu Kα radiation. SEM and TEM images were obtained using a field emission scanning electron microscope (Zeiss Supra55, Germany) and a transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM 2100F, Japan), respectively. XPS studies were carried out on a Thermo Scientific KAlpha apparatus with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source.

sections.heading: 2.4 | Electrochemical measurements
sections.text: A typical H-type cell was used in this study, which contained 80 mL 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (electrolyte) and was equipped with a gas inlet and outlet, allowing the passage of either N2 (99.99%) or CO2 (99.99%) through the solution. A proton exchange membrane (Dupont Nafion 117) was used as the separator between the anodic and cathodic chambers. Electrochemical measurements were conducted with a CHI760E electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua Instruments Co., Ltd., China). The as-prepared electrodes were used as the working electrodes, and a Pt wire and a Ag/AgCl electrode were employed as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The reported potentials were converted to the RHE reference (E (vs RHE) (V) = E (vs Ag/AgCl) (V) + 0.209 V + 0.0591 V × рH). The electrolyte was bubbled with N2 and then CO2 for 30 minutes, respectively, to obtain a CO2-saturated solution with the solution pH decreasing from 8.6 to 7.3. The CO2 bubbling was continued until the end of the measurement.

sections.heading: 2.5 | Product analysis
sections.text:
The HCOO− produced and collected in aqueous electrolyte solutions was analyzed by using ion chromatography (ICS-90, Dionex) with an SI-90G and SI-52 4E Shodex separation column at a flow rate of 0.7 mL/min. The mobile phase was a 3.6 mM Na2CO3 solution. FEHCOO− was calculated from the concentration of HCOO− and the transferred electron quantity by using the following equation33:
FEHCOOH = 2m F I t ð1Þ
where 2 refers to the number of electrons transferred to produce HCOO− from CO2, m is the quantity of HCOO − (moles) product, F is the Faraday constant (96 500 C/mol), I is the current used for the electrolysis, and t is the electrolysis time period.

sections.heading: 3 | RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
In this part, we mainly discuss four kinds of catalysts, namely the catalyst fabricated with both additional MWCNTs and alkali dezincification (abbreviated as SZMC), the catalyst obtained only with alkali dezincification (abbreviated as SZC) or MWCNTs (abbreviated as S0MC), and the one prepared without either additional MWCNTs or alkali dezincification (abbreviated as S0C). The morphologies and structures of these catalyst samples were characterized by using SEM and TEM. The SEM images of SZ0.5MC, S0C, SZC, and S0MC are shown at appropriate magnifications in Figure 1A-D. The morphologies of S0MC and SZ0.5MC samples shown in Figure 1C and D are obviously different from those of S0C and SZC shown in Figure 1A and B. S0C and SZC show a structure with more edges and corners, while S0MC and SZ0.5MC seem smoother, indicating that MWCNTs are well co-electrodeposited with Zn and Sn on the Cu substrate. Furthermore, the TEM image of SZ0.5MC electrode (Figure 1E) shows the uniform deposition of MWCNTs on the copper substrate with a Sn lattice distance of 0.29 nm, which corresponds to the Sn(200) crystal plane. Compared with the relatively flat structure of the S0C and SZC electrodes (Figure 1A and

C) with low porosity, the SZC and SZ0.5MC electrodes (Figure 1B and D) show obvious porous structures after 8 hours of alkaline leaching. These porous electrodes were tested for ERCO2, and the results showed that they did boost the performance due not only to the larger specific surface area, which could be conducive to reactant and intermediate adsorption, but also to the contribution to mass transfer,23,30 thereby reducing the resistance caused by reactant transport and making the reactant more accessible to the active sites.34 Element mapping analysis shown in Figure 1F indicates that MWCNTs and Sn element are successfully deposited on the electrode, although the Sn deposition on MWCNTs is not very uniform. In addition, Zn element is hardly found on the SZ0.5MC electrode, indicating a nearly thorough dezincification by the alkali leaching process.
The XRD patterns were also collected to analyze the crystal structures of the catalysts. In Figure 2A, the XRD pattern of SZ0.5MC electrode is displayed along with those of S0MC, SZC, and S0C for comparison. The XRD patterns
clearly reveal that all Sn and Cu metallic phases in the electrodes have the similar crystal planes but different intensities. Specifically, the diffraction peaks at 43.3 , 50.4 , and 74.1 can be indexed to the (111), (200), and (220) facets of metalic Cu (PDF#99-0034), respectively. The metal Sn exhibits main peaks at 30.6 , 32.0 , 43.9 , 44.9 , and 55.3 , which can be assigned to the (200), (101), (220), (211), and (301) planes of Sn with reference to PDF#86-2264. Thus, these results demonstrate that the metal Sn has been successfully deposited on the Cu substrate. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the intensity of the peak due to the Cu(200) crystal plane is the strongest according to its pattern, but in the case of Sn the intensity of main crystal plane changes under different conditions. In addition, while the peak corresponding to the Sn(200) crystal plane of the S0C electrode is the highest, those from SZC, S0MC, and SZ0.5MC electrodes show relatively consistent height of (200) and (101) planes. Meanwhile, there is no Zn diffraction peak in SZ0.5MC and SZC, suggesting that almost all Zn on the

The valance state of Sn was further confirmed by XPS spectra, and the results are shown in Figures 2B-D, 3 and 4. Based on Figures 2C and 3D-F, it can be seen that the peaks located at 495.5 and 487.2 eV match well with the characteristic peaks assigned to Sn 3d3/2 and Sn 3d5/2, respectively, which clearly confirms the formation of Sn(IV)29,35 on the electrode surface. Two distinct binding energy peaks at 491.7 and 483.1 eV can be observed in Figures 2C and 3D-F, which correspond to Sn 3d3/2 and Sn 3d5/2, respectively, confirming the presence of the Sn(0) species.36,37 Notably, it can be found that all electrodes contain the Sn(IV) species. However, the XRD data shows that Sn(0) is dominant in all of four electrodes. This is because XPS can only detect the valence
state of surface composition and Sn atoms on the electrode surface are easily oxidized in the air and thus form Sn(IV). However, XRD collects signals from the whole material, thus it can be proved that Sn element on the electrode mainly exists in the form of Sn(0), which does not contradict our XPS analysis result. Figures 2B and 3A-C show the XPS results of C 1s in SZ0.5MC, S0MC, SZC, and S0C electrodes. Three distinct binding energies located at 284.8, 286.0, and 288.5 eV can be seen, attributable to C C, C O, and C O, respectively. In addition, a sharp C 1s peak at 284.4 eV can be found in Figures 2B and 3C, which is associated with the added MWCNTs,38,39 but is not present in the SZC and S0C spectra (Figure 3A and B. In addition, we can find very weak characteristic peaks located at 934 eV in Figure 4A, B and D belonging to the Cu species,40,41 but no
characteristic peak of Cu is detected in SZ0.5MC (Figure 4C). Finally, as seen in the Zn 2p spectra (Figures 2D, 3G-I and 4), no characteristic peaks can be observed at about 1021 and 1022 eV,42-44 indicating the absence of Zn in SZC and SZ0.5MC samples.
Electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) can be used to compare the electrochemical activities of different catalysts with different roughness factors.45,46 To estimate the ECSAs of SZ0.5MC, S0MC, SZC, and S0C electrodes, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was carried out in the doublelayer capacitance region between the potentials −0.39 and −0.49 V at different scan rates in N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Figure 5A and B and Figure S1A and B). As shown in Figure 5C and D, the capacitances are 2.3, 0.56, 0.15, and 0.17 mF/cm2 for
SZ0:5MC, S0MC, SZC, and S0C electrodes, respectively. The SZ0.5MC electrode has a capacitance value nearly 4, 15, and 13 times higher than that of S0MC, SZC, and S0C ones, respectively. Combined with Figure 1, it can be concluded that the increase in ECSA is due to both a porous structure caused by alkali leaching and the addition of MWCNTs. SZ0.5MC possesses the largest ECSA, that is, the largest number of active sites, and shows the optimum performance in ERCO2. Especially, there is a slight anomaly in that SZC with a larger specific area displays a lower ECSA than S0C. It may be that the S0C electrode has more corners and edges and these morphologies are also somewhat active for ERCO2.
In order to confirm the activity of SZ0.5MC, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and CV curves were recorded
at two different scan rates of 5 and 50 mV/s in the potential range between 0.51 and −0.99 V (Figure 2). As shown in Figure 2A and B, the maximum current density obtained with CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solutions can reach much higher values (−22.8 mA/cm2) than those in N2-saturated solution, as well as the positive shift of onset potential, demonstrating the better catalytic activity of SZ0.5MC electrode for ERCO2.
The product was detected by ion chromatography and the concentration was further employed to calculate the selectivity of HCOO− production, so as to distinguish the outstanding materials. It can be observed that the FEHCOO− of SZ0.5MC electrode reaches about 91% at −0.99 V, whereas those of S0C, SZC, and S0MC electrodes are 73%, 68%, and 82%, respectively (Figure 6A). These
values of FEHCOO− here correspond to the values of the previously measured ECSA. Thus, such a good performance of SZ0.5MC can be attributed to the larger ECSA with more active sites for ERCO2, along with the 3D porous structure. In addition, the gaseous products of ERCO2 were also analyzed, from which the concentration of CO was found to be around 4% (v/v), with the remaining product being H2. Besides, our experimental results are also compared with those reported in the literature (Table S1), from which the better electrocatalytic ERCO2 performance of SZ0.5MC electrode is confirmed. It is worth noting that some Cu–Sn bimetallic catalysts show slightly higher selectivity than found our study, which can be attributed to the special contribution of Cu to the catalytic performance.36,47,48 On the other hand,
for Sn-based catalysts, SnO2@N-doped porous carbon with the best catalytic performance shows high selectivity (94.1%) and current density (−28.4mA/cm2), but reaction potential is high (−2.2 VAg/AgCl) and an additional ionic liquid is used to increase the conductivity.49 A kind of nanostructured Sn catalysts also shows a higher FEHCOO− of >93%, but the reaction potential is too high (−1.8 VSCE) and the current density is only 5mA/cm
2.50 In our study, we can find that FEHCOO− of 91% and the current density of 20mA/cm2 obtained in stability test are higher than those found in most literature at a lower potential of −0.99 V.
In order to optimize the fabrication process, different synthesis conditions at different component ratios (Sn/Zn), alkali leaching times (tal), quantity of MWCNTs, and electrodeposition current density (jal) were also
investigated; the obtained results are shown in Figure 6BE. From Figure 6B, it can be seen that the ratio Sn:Zn has a slight effect on the catalyst performance, indicated by the fact that there is only an upward trend with a high proportion of Zn content (50:1–20:1), but when the proportion is relatively low (20:1–5:1), the results do not change significantly. Specifically, when the ratio of Sn to Zn is 50:1, FEHCOO− is the lowest (83%). However, when the ratio Sn:Zn reduces to 20:1, 10:1, and 5:1, the value of FEHCOO− is maintained at approximately 91% (91%, 92%, and 92%, respectively). Hence, it can be concluded that the removal of trace amounts of Zn indeed affects the electrode performance due to the increased surface area, but as more Zn is removed, the electrode performance may depend primarily on the properties of the Sn catalyst. Figure 6C shows the effect of alkali leaching time
(tal). It can be seen that when the values of tal are 14, 12, 8, and 4 hours, the values of FEHCOO− correspond to 88%, 92%, 91%, and 90%, respectively, suggesting that tal has only an insignificant effect on the performance when tal is larger than 4 hours. The effect of adding different amounts of MWCNTs on ERCO2 was also investigated,
and the result is shown in Figure 6D. With different amounts of MWCNTs, almost the same results are obtained, indicating that adding more MWCNTs has only an insignificant effect on the selectivity of HCOO− production. In addition, we also studied the influence of tal on the electrocatalytic performance of SZMC electrodes
(Figure 6E). The electrodeposition was carried out at different tal values with corresponding times, namely 40mA for 45minutes, 30mA for 60minutes, and 20mA for 90minutes, respectively. As shown in Figure 6E, jel has only a slight effect on FEHCOO− .
The stability of the catalyst is also a major concern for ERCO2. In order to evaluate the stability of SZ0.5MC electrode, a stability test was conducted at −0.99 V for 10 hours. As shown in Figure 6F, FEHCOO− and the catalytic current density show negligible change during the 10-hour continuous electrolysis, demonstrating excellent catalyst stability in aqueous solutions.

sections.heading: 4 | CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, a nanoporous structured Sn-MWCNT/Cu (SZMC) electrode was fabricated successfully by a facile two-step method. Sn and Zn were co-electrodeposited onto a Cu sheet, which was then leached in an alkaline solution to remove Zn. The formed electrode was used as cathode for ERCO2 to produce HCOO
−. For comparison, several other similar electrodes such as SZC, S0C, and S0MC were also fabricated. Among the different electrodes, the asprepared 3D porous SZ0:5MC electrode gave the best performance with an FEHCOO− of ERCO2 of up to 91% at −0.99 V for 10 hours in 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solutions. This high performance is attributed to the addition of MWCNTs and Zn followed by a chemical dezincification step to create a porous structure with large surface area and then ECSA as well as the resulting favorable intermediate adsorption and mass transfer for enhancing the catalytic activity and selectivity of HCOO− production. In addition, the fabrication method developed in this work can be used for cost-effective and large-scale electrode fabrication for ERCO2 to produce low-carbon fuels.
